units: a mountain route is split into stretches classed by the ground underfoot
the woodland stretch runs in wide bends over soft earth
the slope there stays gentle and even
the scree comes from the rock face broken up by frost
these stones shift underfoot and force quick footwork
the ridge stretch is swept by the wind and narrows in places
the descent leads to a damp gully where water-polished rock is slippery
each stretch calls for its own kit
mapmakers mark these kinds of ground with a graphic symbol
this information lets the walker weigh the effort before setting off
text: Mapmakers break a mountain route into stretches, each one named after the ground you cross. The first is the woodland path, which swings through wide bends over soft earth, and the slope there stays gentle and even. Then comes the scree, where stones prised off the rock face by frost shift under the boot and force you to step quickly and lightly. The third stretch runs along a ridge open to the wind, narrowing in places to little more than the width of a table. The fourth drops towards a damp gully, where the water has polished the rock until it is slippery. Every stretch calls for its own kit: a soft shoe under the trees, a stiff sole on the stones, a light rope near the drop. Hatching on the map marks these surfaces, so that a walker can weigh the effort before setting off.

units: the party left the shelter very early
a veil of mist still lay over the lower valley at the start
the guide had warned that the ford might be cut off if the snow melted quickly
the descent to the river was made without a pause
the river was fuller than the day before
the crossing was arranged in order of increasing weight
a rope was strung between two boulders to make the passage safe
the packs were carried over separately from the heaviest walkers
the party then dried off in an open clearing in the wood
the guide saw the manoeuvre as an ordinary precaution
text: The party left the stone shelter at first light, with mist still lying thick in the bottom of the valley. The guide had warned them the evening before: if the thaw quickened, the ford would be impassable by midday. So they went down to the river without stopping, reaching it as the fog began to tear apart. The water stood higher than the day before, rolling pebbles along with a dull, heavy sound. The crossing was made in order of weight, the lightest first, with a rope strung between two boulders to make the passage safe; the packs went over on their own, apart from the heaviest walkers. It took less time than anyone had feared. On the far bank a clearing gave dry ground, and there each of them wrung out their clothes. The walkers spoke of it afterwards with restrained pride; to the guide it was no more than an ordinary precaution.

units: the angle of the slope must be judged before committing to a mountain flank
the gradient governs the danger
a gentle slope holds its snow in place
a steep slope lets go as soon as it is walked on
a pole serves to test how the layers of snow are stacked
a surface layer shifting over a hardened one means turning back
it is better to move along a rib than in a groove of the ground
a groove gathers moving snow and magnifies it
walkers must go over one at a time so as not to be swept away together
the sound of water under the snow reveals a hollow underfoot
text: Before you commit to a steep flank, judge the angle of the slope, because the angle is what governs the danger. A gentle incline holds its snow in place; a steep one lets go at the first footfall, and the slide carries the walker down with it. Probe the layers with a pole, and if the top layer shifts over a hardened crust, turn back, since that structure is on the point of breaking. Look for a line that follows a rib rather than a groove in the ground, because a groove gathers the moving snow and multiplies its force. Send the party over one at a time, so that a single fall cannot sweep everyone away. Listen, too, for water running beneath the snow: that sound means a hollow underfoot, and a hollow gives way under load. If doubt remains, go back down; turning back costs no more than an extra stretch of walking.

units: the coast path has been losing ground for two seasons
salt spray and swell are hollowing out the rock face from below
walkers use the stretch all the same
the warning sign is regularly hidden by the plants
the person in charge of the paths admits that the ban has failed
a fresh line has been set out further from the sea in the low scrub
this line has steps and a wooden handrail
walkers choose it for its comfort and not out of obedience
the old stretch is closing over on its own under the scrub
the warden reckons a better offer beats a telling-off
text: For two seasons now the coast path has been losing ground, eaten away by spray and by the swell that hollows out the cliff from underneath. Walkers use it all the same. The view is good, the going is easy, and the warning sign keeps vanishing under the undergrowth. The warden in charge of the paths admits it without hedging: banning people did not work, they have tried that. So they tried something else. A fresh line has been pegged out further back, in the low scrub, with steps cut into the ground and a wooden handrail. People take it because it is more comfortable, not because they have been told to. Meanwhile the threatened stretch is quietly closing over under the thorn bushes. You gain nothing by telling walkers off, she says with a shrug; you gain by offering them something better.

units: two valleys on either side of the same range have very little in common
the eastern valley is wide and flat
its river loops slowly through it and carries silt
grassland comes down to the water's edge there
the western valley forms a narrow cut
a fast stream drops from pool to pool there and throws up foam
the sides carry scattered trees clinging to the rock
the difference comes from the steepness of the ground
ground that is almost level lets the river wander
the first valley is walked without effort while the second is climbed
text: Two valleys lie on either side of the same mountain range, and they have almost nothing in common with each other. The eastern one opens out flat and wide, and its river loops slowly through it, silent, brown with silt, while grassland runs right down to the water's edge. The western one is a narrow cut in the rock: a fast stream drops from pool to pool, white with foam, and thin trees cling to the sides wherever they can find a hold. The difference comes down to the steepness of the ground. Where the ground barely falls, the river takes its time and spreads into bends; where it plunges, the water runs straight and digs. Walkers feel it in their legs. The first valley is strolled through, the second is climbed like a staircase. Two neighbouring landscapes, two ways of wearing down the rock.

units: the author speaks of what is felt before a line of peaks veiled in mist
he blames packaged travel for working like a tick-list
he offers three ways of giving up a fixed programme
the first is to move very slowly
stopping when the shade takes over belongs to this first way
the second is to walk the same path again at another time of year
this return shows that the colours the sounds and the smells have changed
the third is to ignore the names of the peaks on purpose
the author refuses to treat a landscape as something to be hoarded
he sets the one who agrees to dawdle against the one who comes to take stock
text: Who has never stood before a ridge drowned in mist and felt that the eye was after something more than a picture? Travel, as it is sold to us, comes in lists: a viewpoint, a lake, a photogenic clearing, and one ticks them off. I want to argue for three ways of losing your route. The first is slowness: walking at the pace of a grazing herd, stopping wherever the shade settles. The second is return: coming back to the same path in the opposite season and finding that its colours, its sounds and its smells have all changed. The third is chosen ignorance: not learning the names of the peaks beforehand, letting them stand as pure shapes. A landscape is not a thing to be collected. It gives itself to anyone willing to lose an afternoon in it, and shuts against anyone who comes to take stock.

units: the path maintenance worker started out carrying stone for his elder
his first jobs were physical ones
he had to clear away rockfall that had come down on the track

he was then given the setting of the waymarks
a badly placed marker can send a walker over a drop
he was trained in fitting stone without mortar
he built a first retaining wall under someone else's supervision
he now lays out the routes himself working out the acceptable gradient and the run-off
he teaches his learners that a path the water leaves cleanly looks after itself
text: The man who keeps the paths in repair learned the trade by carrying stone for the man before him. His first jobs were the heavy ones: clearing away rockfall that had spilled onto the track, laying wooden drains across the slope, scouring out the channels. Waymarking came later, and it asked more of him, since a badly placed marker sends a walker over a drop. He was trained in fitting stone without mortar, then built his first retaining wall under another man's eye. These days he lays out the routes himself, working out what gradient the ground will take, turning the path so that the water leaves it instead of following it, choosing where the footing goes. Now he trains learners of his own in turn, and the first lesson he passes on fits in a single line: a well-drained path mends itself.

units: the book deals with high mountain paths and carries conviction
its quality follows from a method the author owns up to
he walked in person every route he presents
he covered them at different times of year
the times given can therefore be trusted

the book points in particular to seeping rock a ford swollen by rain and a scree slope loosened by the thaw
the reader comes away better equipped and more careful
the photographs are faulted for showing nothing but clear skies
this visual choice makes the route look too reassuring
text: The book on high mountain paths carries conviction, and its success rests first of all on a method the author owns up to. He walked every route he sets out, and walked them at every time of year; the times he gives can therefore be trusted, and first-hand experience brings out dangers that no survey map would ever show. So the descriptions point to the place where the rock seeps, to the ford that swells after rain, to the band of scree that loosens in a thaw. The reader comes away better equipped and, in consequence, more careful. The photographs are another matter: taken under clear skies, they leave out the mist that governs half of these outings. The choice weakens the argument, because it makes the route look kinder than it is. The book instructs; it reassures rather too quickly.

units: the writer doubts that his previous message was sent on
the village postbox looked as though it had not been emptied
he is writing from an inn down in a valley
his stay has run on beyond what he had planned
his boots gave out on the third mountain pass
the vehicle meant to take him back does not run outside the busy season
he first thought of giving up his trip
the innkeeper found him a driver who delivers goods to the next town
a tradesman resoled his boots cheaply
he announces a departure two stages earlier than planned
text: I hope my last card reached you in the end, though the village postbox looked as if nobody had come to empty it in an age. I am writing from an inn down in the valley, where I have stayed on rather longer than I meant to. Two things went wrong: my boots gave out on the third pass, and the coach that was meant to bring me back does not run outside the busy season. At first I thought I would have to give up and make my own way home. The innkeeper had another idea. His brother-in-law drives down every week with crates for the next town along, and he is glad to take me. In the meantime a cobbler has fitted fresh soles to my boots for very little. So I set off the day after tomorrow, two stages shorter and one story richer. Write to the return address; I shall pick up the post when I arrive.

units: visitor numbers vary a great deal from one time of year to another
the gap is not where you would imagine it
in the warm months visitors come in large numbers
they gather on a very small number of waymarked routes
they move about little and take an enormous number of pictures
in the cold months visitors are few but spread out away from the paths
it is these scattered visitors who do the most damage
ground trampled by a group recovers
a walker crossing a clearing in the wood upsets the breeding of the birds
the warden favours opening further routes and putting up explanatory signs over penalties
text: Does the number of visitors change from one season to the next? Hugely, says the warden, but not in the way you would expect. In the warm months they arrive in crowds and stay bunched on three or four waymarked paths; they walk very little and photograph endlessly. In the cold months there are hardly any of them, but they go everywhere, off the paths included. And which group causes the trouble? The second, no question. A herd of walkers on a path packs the soil down, and soil recovers. One person cutting across a clearing disturbs the nesting birds, and that does not recover. So what is done about it? The warden would rather widen the choice: further routes opened in the quiet months, and signs that tell the story of a nest instead of forbidding things. And does it work? Better than fines, she says, laughing.
